iconic_games_note: BMO Field has genuine, deep football history: home of MLS club Toronto FC since 2007 and an intermittent home of the Canada men's national team; it hosted the 2007 FIFA U-20 World Cup (incl. the final, Argentina 2–1 Czech Republic) and the 2014 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup, MLS Cup finals in 2010, 2016 and 2017, and high-profile club friendlies (Real Madrid 2009). The June 12, 2026 Canada–Bosnia match was the first men's World Cup match ever played in Canada. The curated 2026 World Cup scores above are for matches already played as of the 2026-06-23 snapshot; the remaining group games (e.g. Panama–Croatia June 23, Senegal–Iraq June 26) and the July 2 Round of 32 match were upcoming/unplayed and so are not listed with scores. Non-football events of note (clearly NOT football): the venue also hosts the CFL's Toronto Argonauts and staged the 104th Grey Cup (Nov 27, 2016) and the NHL Centennial Classic outdoor hockey game (Jan 1, 2017, attendance 40,148).

city_history.founded: Incorporated as the City of Toronto on March 6, 1834 (the restored Indigenous-derived name replacing 'York', the settlement founded 1793 by Lt.-Gov. John Graves Simcoe as the capital of Upper Canada)
city_history.significance: Toronto is the most populous city in Canada and the capital of Ontario, with a 2021 census population of 2,794,356 (4th-most-populous city in North America after Mexico City, New York and Los Angeles). It is Canada's financial and cultural centre and one of the most multicultural cities in the world. BMO Field sits at Exhibition Place on the Lake Ontario waterfront. Toronto is one of only two Canadian 2026 World Cup host cities, the other being Vancouver.
city_history.football_culture: Toronto has a deep, established football (soccer) culture anchored at BMO Field itself: it is the home of MLS side Toronto FC (founded 2007), whose treble-winning 2017 MLS Cup victory at the ground drew a passionate sellout, and an intermittent home of the Canada men's national team. The venue's purpose-built soccer pedigree (2007 FIFA U-20 World Cup, 2014 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup, marquee club friendlies vs Real Madrid and others) and the city's large immigrant communities give the host its football identity directly — no metro-proxy needed (this is a genuine soccer-specific venue, not a suburban NFL site).

stadium_history_facts: Broke ground March 29, 2006; opened April 28, 2007, built as a soccer-specific stadium for the 2007 FIFA U-20 World Cup and as the first home of Toronto FC; original construction cost CA$62.9 million (confirmed in pinned Wikipedia infobox).
Originally surfaced with FieldTurf (2007–2009), which drew player criticism; converted to natural Kentucky bluegrass before the 2010 season, then to a hybrid-grass system from 2019.

Underwent a major 2014–2016 expansion (~CA$120M, designed by Gensler): added an east-grandstand upper deck (Phase 1, ~8,400 seats, completed May 2015) and a canopy roof over east/west/south stands plus a lengthened field for Canadian football, raising soccer capacity from ~21,566 to ~30,000 (confirmed via Gensler project page and press).
The CFL's Toronto Argonauts moved in for the 2016 season; BMO Field hosted the 104th Grey Cup (Nov 27, 2016).
Hosted the NHL Centennial Classic outdoor game on Jan 1, 2017 (attendance 40,148).
Hosted MLS Cup finals in 2010 (neutral site), 2016 and 2017 (Toronto FC as host); the 2017 final delivered Toronto FC the title and a domestic treble.

Bank of Montreal (BMO) holds naming rights; the stadium is temporarily renamed 'Toronto Stadium' for the 2026 World Cup under FIFA's clean-venue/anti-sponsor policy (it was likewise 'National Soccer Stadium' for the 2007 and 2014 FIFA youth tournaments).
For the 2026 World Cup it hosts six matches — five group-stage games plus one Round of 32 (July 2, 2026) — including Canada's opener on June 12, 2026.
